newsitem.title: UK: Britain condemns suspect N.Irish guerrilla bomb.
newsitem.headline: Britain condemns suspect N.Irish guerrilla bomb.

text.p: Britain condemned IRA guerrillas on Wednesday for leaving a suspected bomb near a Belfast hotel packed with New Year revellers.

Northern Ireland Secretary Sir Patrick Mayhew described the alert as "a New Year message" from what he called criminal gangsters who had not turned away from a strategy of violence to achieve their political objectives. Vowing not to appease the Irish Republican Army that is fighting to end British rule, Mayhew told BBC radio:" I reject that message with disgust and contempt on behalf of the government and all the decent people of Northern Ireland."
British security forces sealed off parkland around Belfast Castle, a 19th century former private mansion, as bomb disposal officers tried to establish if an abandonded vehicle contained explosives.
Police said a man using an IRA identity codeword had telephoned the media late on Tuesday saying there was a landmine in the vehicle.
He said they had dumped the vehicle in the grounds of Belfast Castle after encountering high-level British counter-guerrilla activity. The premises were evacuated.
Security sources said if the warning were genuine it could mean that the guerrillas had been thwarted in plans to stage an attack in the early hours of New Year's Day.
Police said officers on high alert during renewed tension had already become suspicious of a van parked in the hotel grounds and called in the bomb squad.
A bride and groom, their guests and others attending New Year's Eve receptions were among those led out of the building.
David Trimble, leader of the Ulster Unionist Party, which speaks for most of the province's Protestant majority who firm support rule from London, said the IRA was wedded to violence.

"There have been several attempts at major terrorist attacks in Northern Ireland (in recent months). It underlines the complete fatuity of the suggestions that there was about to be a ceasefire," he told BBC radio.
"There's no indication whatsoever that the IRA are contemplating politics, every indication that they are trying to step up their activity."
Security has been stepped up across Northern Ireland and in mainland Britain since the IRA abandoned a ceasefire last February in a 27-year campaign to end British rule.
The IRA set off a wave of bombs in British cities and killed a soldier at British army headquarters south of Belfast last October, dashing hopes of an early end to violence.

Tension increased recently with signs that pro-British Loyalist guerrillas might end a two-year truce. Booby trap bombs were placed under cars belonging to senior republicans, injuring one of them. Loyalist hardliners were blamed.
